Overview

Stage 2 has 7 questions in 3 tasks plus two submissions (a 10 to 15 minute video with photos, and a final P&ID). Q3.1 and Q3.2 are pure theory and are fully answered below; every other question is an experiment, so this guide gives the exact procedure, the formulas, the expected numbers to sanity-check against, and the blank table to fill.

Task Question Type What you hand in
1 Hydraulics design Q1.1 Build and P&ID, Case 1 and Case 2 Build + demo P&ID, code, flow vs time trend, total litres, video
1 Hydraulics design Q1.2 Run at 1, 3 and 6 L/min Experiment + theory Theoretical vs actual velocity table
2 Valve response Q2.1 Valve at 25, 50, 75, 100 % Experiment Table + graph of position vs flow
2 Valve response Q2.2 Calibration Q = a·f + b Analysis of Q2.3 data a, b, R², max and average error
2 Valve response Q2.3 Five pulse/volume trials Experiment Trial table
3 Theory Q3.1 Residence time Theory Answered in full below
3 Theory Q3.2 Fault table A to E Theory Answered in full below

Fixed numbers used throughout: pipe ID 8 mm (area 5.027 × 10⁻⁵ m²), water ρ = 1000 kg/m³, µ = 1 × 10⁻³ Pa·s, target 3 L/min. Pumps: 12 V, 2.5 to 3.5 A, 6.1 L/min free flow, 135 psi cutoff. FT-01 is a YF-S401 Hall-effect turbine sensor, 0.3 to 6 L/min, nominal datasheet factor f (Hz) ≈ 98 × Q (L/min), so about 5880 pulses per litre. Treat 98 only as a starting value: the paper explicitly requires you to calibrate it.

Do the questions in this order, not the paper's order: build (Q1.1 hardware) → Q2.3 trials → Q2.2 calibration → load the calibrated a and b into the firmware → Q2.1 → Q1.2 → Case 1 and Case 2 demo and video. Every flow number in Q1.1, Q1.2 and Q2.1 depends on the calibration, so calibrating first saves redoing those runs. The firmware itself is being written in the sibling thread "ESP32 flow skid firmware"; this guide only says what each question needs it to log.

Setup and wiring

Build the agreed skid exactly as in the Stage 2 Flow Skid drawing (Q1.1 below shows it), then leak-test with water before any electronics are connected.

Electrical connections on the custom PCB

PCB connector Connects to Notes
12V INPUT 12 V DC SMPS (+ and −) Check polarity with a meter before plugging in. The board has a 40 A blade fuse (U5).
P1, P2, P3 (12 V power for motor drivers) B+ / B− of BTS7960 #1, #2, #3 One driver per pump: #1 = P-01 transfer, #2 = P-02 return, #3 = P-03 flush.
U2, U3, U4 (top three headers) Logic header of BTS7960 #1, #2, #3 (VCC, GND, R_EN, L_EN, RPWM, LPWM; the IS current-sense pins are not routed on this PCB) Pumps run one way only: PWM on RPWM, LPWM held low, both EN high.
BTS7960 M+ / M− Pump red / black leads Pump direction matters: a reversed diaphragm pump does not pump.
SOLENOID_VALVE (S/V/G) D4184 MOSFET module → SOV-01 coil (12 V DC) Fit a 1N4007 across the coil, stripe to +12 V.
FLOW_SENSOR (S/V/G) YF-S401: yellow = S, red = V, black = G Arrow on the sensor body must point toward TK-01.
FLOAT_SWITCH (FSW/GND) Float switch LS-01 in the sump's second top hole Mount it at the "high" level you want P-01 to stop at.
ON/OFF_SWITCH (SW/GND) Red tact switch, diagonal legs Starts Case 1.

The GPIO number behind each connector is fixed by the PCB traces; the sibling firmware thread maps them, so wire to the connectors and do not rewire pins.

Power budget

Three pumps at up to 3.5 A plus the solenoid (about 0.5 A) draw about 11 A in Case 2, when everything runs together. The SMPS should be rated at least 15 A (180 W); if it is smaller, Case 2 is where it will brown out and reset the ESP32.

Before first power-on

  1. Teflon tape on every threaded joint (brass bulkheads B1 to B5, ball valves, solenoid).
  2. Pump flow direction: inlet and outlet are on the rear face (the circled photo in Hardware kit/Safety). Inlet must face the supply tank.
  3. Flow sensor arrow points downstream, toward TK-01.
  4. Wire sleeves on every exposed joint; keep 12 V wiring away from the wet side.
  5. Fill TK-01 to about 5 L (headroom for the 4.2 L flush, see Q1.1), open BV-03 and BV-01, keep BV-02 closed, and check every joint for drips for 5 minutes with the pumps off.
  6. Never fully close BV-01 while P-02 runs. The pump only cuts off at 135 psi (9.3 bar), which is above the YF-S401's 0.8 MPa rating and enough to blow a push-fit tube off. Task 2's lowest setting is 25 %, so you never need it shut.
  7. Do not let P-02 run dry for long; the firmware's flow-zero check (see Case 2) also protects it.

Task 1: Hydraulic system design

Q1.1 Hydraulic path, P&ID, Case 1 and Case 2

The P&ID is already drawn: use the two figures below (also in Stage 2/Figures as fig_c1.png and fig_c2.png) as the submitted sketch and the "Final P&ID block diagram". Redraw by hand on page 4 of the paper with the same tags if a hand sketch is required.

Tag list to write on the P&ID. The paper asks for needle valves, but the kit has none, so BV-01 (ball valve) is the throttle; say so in a note on the sketch.

Tag Item Where it sits
TK-01 10 L process fluid tank Outlet bottom (B1), return inlet top (B2)
BV-03 Ball valve, maintenance shut-off TK-01 outlet, open while running
SOV-01 (XV-01) 12 V DC on/off solenoid After BV-03; isolates TK-01 in Case 2
T-01 8 mm equal tee After SOV-01; flush line joins here
P-01 Transfer pump, 50 % PWM T-01 to sump inlet (B3, top)
TK-02 Sump, 4.2 L Inlet top, float switch top, outlet bottom (B4)
LS-01 Float switch, sump high level Sump second top hole
P-02 Return pump, 100 % PWM Sump outlet to BV-01
BV-01 Ball valve, throttle P-02 discharge, sets flow for Task 2 and the 3 L/min target

P-03 Flush pump BV-02 to T-01

Mark on the sketch: flow arrows on every line, "8 mm ID tube" on the lines, measurement points FT-01 (flow) and LS-01 (level), and the control signals as dashed lines to the ESP32 PCB.

Water inventory (do this before filling). In Case 2 all 4.2 L of flush water ends up in TK-01, and in Case 1 the "external charge" water does too. Start with no more than about 5 L in TK-01 so the 10 L tank cannot overflow.

Commissioning: balance the two pumps. P-01 at 50 % and P-02 at 100 % will not move the same flow on their own. Run Case 1 and watch the sump for 2 minutes. If the level falls, P-02 will soon suck air (flow goes intermittent, exactly condition E in Q3.2), so close BV-01 a little. If it rises to the float, open BV-01. Aim for a steady sump level with FT-01 near 3 L/min, which also meets the 3 L/min target.

Case 1 demo.

  1. Press the ON/OFF switch. SOV-01 opens, P-01 starts at 50 %, P-02 at 100 %.
  2. Let it run 2 to 3 minutes so the flow trend is steady at about 3 L/min.
  3. Pour about 1 L of water quickly into the sump (the "sudden external charge"). LS-01 trips: P-01 must stop and P-02 must keep running.
  4. P-02 drains the sump; when LS-01 drops, P-01 restarts and the loop continues. The firmware holds P-01 off until the float has stayed clear for 3 s, so a sloshing float does not chatter the pump.
  5. Screenshots: the live flow in L/min, the flow vs time trend in mL/s (mL/s = L/min × 1000 / 60, so 3 L/min = 50 mL/s), and the totalized litres returned to TK-01. The firmware thread is set up to print these over serial; plot with the Arduino/PlatformIO serial plotter or save the CSV and plot it.
  6. Expect the flow trace to dip slightly while P-01 is stopped only if the sump level falls a lot; P-02's flow is set mainly by BV-01, so a flat trace through the event is the correct result.

Case 2 demo (runs straight on from Case 1 in one go).

  1. After 300 s of Case 1 (firmware setting c1time), the firmware closes SOV-01 to isolate TK-01 and starts a 20 s countdown on serial to open BV-02 (bvtime; typing next skips the wait).
  2. Open BV-02 by hand. This is the only manual action allowed.
  3. P-03 starts and all three pumps run together; flush water goes TK-03 → P-03 → T-01 → P-01 → sump → P-02 → FT-01 → TK-01.
  4. When TK-03 is empty, P-03 and P-01 deliver air, the sump drains, and FT-01 falls to zero. The firmware treats a sustained near-zero flow (5 s below 0.15 L/min, checked only after the first 20 s of flushing, with a 600 s safety cap) as "flush supply exhausted" and switches every pump off and leaves SOV-01 closed. The totalizer should read roughly 4.2 L for the flush phase, which is a good cross-check to show in the video.

Code to submit. Submit Stage 2/Codes pspss/Lam Stage 2/src/main.cpp from the "ESP32 flow skid firmware" thread.

Q1.2 Operate at 1, 3 and 6 L/min and compare with theory

Theory (fill these numbers in directly). Mean velocity v = Q / A with A = πD²/4 = 5.027 × 10⁻⁵ m² for D = 8 mm. Re = ρvD/µ. Friction loss per metre uses Blasius, f = 0.316 Re−0.25, for Re above 2300.

Q (L/min) Q (m³/s) v (m/s) Re Regime f Δp per metre of tube (Pa/m) Expected FT-01 frequency (Hz, at 98 × Q) Bubble transit time over 2 m (s)
1 1.667 × 10⁻⁵ 0.33 2653 Transitional 0.044 about 300 98 6.0
3 5.000 × 10⁻⁵ 0.99 7958 Turbulent 0.034 about 2070 294 2.0
6 1.000 × 10⁻⁴ 1.99 15915 Turbulent 0.028 about 6960 588 1.0

Loss grows roughly with Q1.75, so 6 L/min costs about 23 times the loss of 1 L/min per metre of tube.

Experiment.

  1. Use the Case 1 loop. Set each flow with the firmware's flow <L/min> serial command, which runs a PI loop on P-02's PWM (throttling BV-01 also works), until the calibrated FT-01 reading holds steady at 1, 3 and 6 L/min. Record 60 s of readings at each and take the mean and the min/max spread.
  2. Actual mean velocity = measured Q / A.
  3. Independent check: mark two points 2 m apart on a straight run of the return tube, let a small air bubble (or a drop of food colouring) pass and time it with a phone slow-motion video. v_bubble = 2 m / time.
  4. Measure the real tube inner diameter with a vernier. The kit tube is 10 mm OD; if the ID is not 8 mm, velocity scales with 1/D², so a 6.5 mm ID gives 1.5 times the velocity in the table. State which diameter you used.

What to write in the comparison.

  • 6 L/min is at the sensor's upper limit and at the pump's 6.1 L/min free-flow rating. With the sensor, valve and 1 to 2 m of 8 mm tube in the line, P-02 will very likely top out below 6 L/min. Record the maximum you actually reached and explain it with the loss column above; that is a correct engineering result, not a failure.
  • At 1 L/min the flow is transitional and near the bottom of the sensor's 0.3 to 6 L/min range, so expect a noisier reading and a larger calibration error.
  • A bubble rides near the centre of the tube, where the fluid moves faster than the mean: about 1.2 times the mean in turbulent flow and up to 2 times in laminar flow. So v_bubble above v_mean is expected, more so at 1 L/min.
  • The diaphragm pumps pulse, so the instantaneous flow ripples around the mean; report the spread as well as the mean.

Task 2: Flow response to valve position

Q2.3 Five pulse and volume trials (do this first)

This gives the raw data for Q2.2, so it comes before the other Task 2 runs. You need a measuring jug of at least 2 L, or better, a bucket on a kitchen scale (1 g of water = 1 mL), and a stopwatch or the firmware's own timer.

  1. Open the serial monitor. Type trial start and trial stop to bracket each trial; the firmware prints N, t and f. Then type trial vol <litres> to record the collected volume.
  2. Take the FT-01 return tube out of TK-01's top hole and hold it over a spare bucket.
  3. Set BV-01 for the first condition and run P-02 until the flow is steady.
  4. In one motion, swing the tube into the measuring container and start the count. After 30 to 60 s (or at least 1 L), swing it out and stop the count.
  5. Read the collected volume V. Compute f = N / t and actual Q = V / t × 60 (L/min).
  6. Pour the water back into TK-01 after each trial so the sump and tank never run low.
  7. Repeat for five BV-01 positions spread over the range, aiming for roughly 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 L/min. Two repeats per condition make the calibration much more convincing.

Q2.2 Calibration equation Q = a·f + b

Fit a straight line through the five (f, Q) points from Q2.3 by least squares. In Excel or Sheets: a = SLOPE(Q, f), b = INTERCEPT(Q, f), R² = RSQ(Q, f), or add a linear trendline with "display equation and R²". By hand:

For each trial, Q̂ᵢ = a·fᵢ + b is the fitted flow and the calibration error is eᵢ = |Q̂ᵢ − Qᵢ| / Qᵢ × 100 %. Maximum calibration error = the largest eᵢ; average calibration error = the mean of the five eᵢ.

# paste your five trials, run with python3
f = [ , , , , ]   # Hz
Q = [ , , , , ]   # L/min
n = len(f); Sf, SQ = sum(f), sum(Q)
a = (n*sum(x*y for x, y in zip(f, Q)) - Sf*SQ) / (n*sum(x*x for x in f) - Sf**2)
b = (SQ - a*Sf) / n
Qh = [a*x + b for x in f]; Qm = SQ / n
R2 = 1 - sum((q-h)**2 for q, h in zip(Q, Qh)) / sum((q-Qm)**2 for q in Q)
e = [abs(h-q)/q*100 for q, h in zip(Q, Qh)]
print(f"a={a:.5f} L/min/Hz  b={b:.3f} L/min  R2={R2:.4f}  max={max(e):.2f}%  avg={sum(e)/n:.2f}%")

What to expect, so you can spot a bad trial: a close to 1/98 = 0.0102 L/min per Hz (±10 % is normal for these sensors), b within about ±0.1 L/min, R² above 0.99, average error a few percent. A trial far off the line usually means a timing slip when swinging the tube; redo it rather than keep it.

Then put a and b into the firmware. Type fit to get a, b, R² and the errors from the recorded trials, and fit save to store them in flash (or set them with seta / setb). The firmware computes flow = a·f + b and forces it to 0 when f = 0, so a positive b never reports flow with the pump off. Volume totalized back to TK-01 = the sum of flow × Δt over each sample period.

Q2.1 Valve position 25, 50, 75 and 100 %

A ball valve is a quarter-turn valve: 0° is shut and 90° is fully open, so position % = handle angle / 90°. Print or draw a protractor arc, tape it under BV-01's handle, and mark 22.5° (25 %), 45° (50 %), 67.5° (75 %) and 90° (100 %). The paper's table says 70 % (63°) while the question says 75 %; do 75 % and add a 70 % reading too so either marking scheme is covered.

  1. Run the Case 1 loop with the calibrated firmware, P-02 at 100 %.
  2. Start at 100 % and step down to 25 %, always approaching each mark from the same direction so handle play does not shift the reading.
  3. At each mark wait about 30 s for the flow to settle, then average 30 s of readings. Keep the flow vs time log running: each step shows as a clean staircase, and that same log is the "flow vs time data" the paper asks you to record and analyse.
  4. At low openings P-01 will overfill the sump and the float will stop it; that is fine, it is the level protection working.
  5. Plot valve position (%) on x against flow (L/min) on y and draw a smooth curve through the points.

What the graph will show and how to explain it. Flow will not be proportional to position. A ball valve has a quick-opening characteristic: most of the flow arrives in the first 30 to 50 % of travel, and between 75 % and 100 % the flow barely changes because the pump, the 8 mm tubing and FT-01 now set the flow, not the valve. Conclude that a ball valve gives coarse control near the low end and almost none near full open, which is why a needle or globe valve (or pump PWM) is the better way to hold an exact 3 L/min. Never take a 0 % point with P-02 running (see the safety note in Setup).

Task 3: Theory and fault analysis (answers)

Q3.1 Residence time

Answer: Tr = 12 s. The paper prints Tr = Q/V, but that has units of 1/time (5 per minute here). Residence time is volume divided by flow, so write the corrected formula and note the typo:

  1. What it represents. The average time a fluid element spends inside that tube section, from entering to leaving. Equivalently, the time needed to replace the section's whole 0.5 L contents once at the operating flow.
  2. Tubing volume doubled, same flow. Tr doubles to 24 s, because Tr is proportional to V.
  3. Flow doubled, same volume. Tr halves to 6 s, because Tr is inversely proportional to Q.
  4. Why it matters for a sudden flow change. In a liquid-full, rigid line, a change in flow rate travels at nearly the speed of sound in water, so FT-01 sees a pump or valve change almost at once. Anything carried by the fluid itself (an air slug, debris, the flush front, a temperature or concentration change) only reaches FT-01 after about Tr. So a sudden step in measured flow points to a hydraulic event (valve, pump, blockage) or a sensor fault, while a disturbance that appears roughly Tr after an upstream event is something transported by the fluid. Residence time also sets how long a flush must run: several residence times are needed before the old process fluid is displaced from a section. Tanks such as the sump add their own much longer residence time (4.2 L at 3 L/min is about 84 s), which is why level changes lag behind pump changes.

Q3.2 Fault diagnosis from FT-01

Condition Pump Valve FT-01 signal Most likely cause
A ON Open Normal Healthy system, normal operation. Use as the baseline.
B ON Partly closed Reduced Expected response to valve restriction: added valve loss moves the pump to a lower flow on its curve. If the valve were actually fully open, the same signature would mean a partial blockage, a clogging strainer or a weakening pump.
C ON Open Zero No flow reaching or turning the sensor despite a running command. Candidates: hydraulic blockage or a closed valve elsewhere (for example SOV-01 not opening), pump failure (motor or driver fault, air-locked or dry pump, empty supply tank), or sensor/signal failure (jammed rotor, broken signal wire, lost 5 V).
D OFF Open Zero Normal and expected: no pump, no flow. Not a fault, and it confirms the sensor has no false pulses at rest.
E ON Open Intermittent Unstable flow or a bad signal. Hydraulic: air entering the suction (low sump or tank level, loose suction fitting), cavitation, or a pump starved by an unbalanced loop. Instrumentation: a loose connector or broken wire on the signal line, electrical noise, or debris catching the rotor.

Hardest to distinguish with FT-01 alone: condition C. Zero pulses look identical whether the pump has failed, the line is blocked, or the sensor has died, because FT-01 only reports that its rotor is not turning. (E is the runner-up: real flow fluctuation and a flickering signal wire look the same.)

Extra information that separates them:

  • Pump motor current. This needs extra instrumentation: the BTS7960 has IS current-sense outputs, but this PCB's driver headers do not carry them, so add a clamp meter or an inline current sensor such as an ACS712. High current with zero flow means the pump is pushing against a blockage or closed valve. Near-zero current means the pump, motor or driver has failed. Normal current points to a sensor fault.
  • Discharge pressure after the pump: high pressure means blockage, low pressure means pump failure, normal pressure with zero pulses means the sensor.
  • Level changes: if the sump level is falling while FT-01 reads zero, water is clearly moving and FT-01 is at fault. The float switch and visual tank levels give this for free.
  • Direct checks: see water arriving at TK-01's return, measure the sensor's 5 V supply and look at the signal pin on a scope or a multimeter's frequency range, and confirm the solenoid's actual state.
  • For E, comparing pump current with the flow trace helps: a steady current with a flickering flow suggests the signal wiring, while current dips in step with the flow dips suggest air or cavitation.

Save each run's log with tools/flow_logger.py in the firmware folder, which also plots it, so every graph comes from the same raw data.

Background: the ideas behind this guide

Everything above rests on about a dozen ideas from fluid mechanics, electronics and statistics. This section explains each from scratch, in the order they build on each other, and says which question uses it. No prior engineering knowledge is assumed beyond school physics.

1. What the system is and why it exists

Chip factories move liquids (ultrapure water, acids, solvents, polishing slurries) from large supply tanks to the machines that process silicon wafers. If the flow is wrong, the chemistry on the wafer is wrong and the wafers are scrapped, so factories measure flow constantly and react when it drifts. Your kit is a tabletop version of that: a supply tank, pumps that move the liquid, a sensor that measures how much is moving, a controller that switches things on and off, and a return path back to the tank. A frame-mounted package like this is called a skid. The challenge asks you to do what a factory engineer does: set a flow, measure it, notice when it goes wrong, work out why, and recover.

2. Flow rate, velocity and units

Flow rate (Q) is the volume of liquid passing a point per unit of time. Velocity (v) is how fast the liquid itself moves, in metres per second. They are linked by the cross-sectional area of the tube (A):

For the 8 mm tube, A = 50.3 mm² = 5.03 × 10⁻⁵ m². Squeeze the same flow through a narrower tube and the water has to move faster; this is why the tube's real inner diameter matters so much in Q1.2.

Quantity Equals
1 L 1000 mL = 0.001 m³ = 1 kg of water
1 L/min 16.67 mL/s = 1.667 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s
3 L/min (target) 50 mL/s, about 1 m/s in an 8 mm tube

Water is practically incompressible. Whatever goes into one end of a full tube comes out the other end at the same moment, so in a single loop the flow is the same at every point in series. In a tank, the level changes by the difference between what flows in and what flows out (a mass balance): if P-01 delivers more than P-02 removes, the sump fills; if less, it empties. That one idea explains the sump-balancing step in Q1.1 and the float switch logic.

3. Density, viscosity and the Reynolds number

Density (ρ) is mass per volume: water is 1000 kg/m³, which is just 1 kg per litre. Viscosity (µ) is a liquid's internal stickiness, its resistance to layers sliding past each other: honey is very viscous, water barely (1 × 10⁻³ Pa·s).

The Reynolds number compares the liquid's momentum (which tends to make it swirl) with its viscosity (which tends to keep it orderly). It has no units:

Re Regime What it looks like
below about 2300 Laminar Smooth parallel layers, like syrup pouring. The centre moves twice as fast as the average.
2300 to 4000 Transitional Flickers between the two. Your 1 L/min run (Re about 2650) sits here.
above about 4000 Turbulent Chaotic eddies mixing the flow. Your 3 and 6 L/min runs. Velocity is nearly uniform across the tube.

The regime changes how much pressure friction costs (next idea) and how evenly the water hits the flow sensor's rotor, which is one reason sensors are least accurate at the low end of their range.

4. Pressure and pressure loss

Pressure is force per unit area. Units you will meet:

Unit Equals
1 Pa (pascal) 1 N/m², tiny
1 kPa 1000 Pa
1 bar 100 kPa, about atmospheric pressure
1 psi (pound per square inch) 6.9 kPa; 14.5 psi = 1 bar
135 psi (pump cutoff) 9.3 bar
0.8 MPa (sensor rating) 8 bar

Pushing water through a tube costs pressure, because the water rubs on the walls and churns internally. This pressure loss (also called head loss) is given by the Darcy–Weisbach equation:

Here L is the tube length, D its diameter and f the friction factor, a number that depends on Re: f = 64 / Re for laminar flow, and roughly f = 0.316 Re−0.25 (the Blasius formula) for turbulent flow in a smooth tube. Every valve, tee, bend and the flow sensor adds its own extra loss on top. The key takeaway is that loss grows steeply with flow, roughly with Q²: double the flow and you need about three to four times the pressure.

5. Pumps and the operating point

A pump adds pressure to the liquid. The kit's pumps are 12 V diaphragm pumps: the motor wobbles a rubber membrane, and one-way flaps (check valves) make each stroke push water forward only. Three practical consequences follow. The flow pulses with each stroke rather than being perfectly smooth. The pump is self-priming, meaning it can suck air out of its inlet line and pull water up to itself. And it carries a pressure switch that cuts the motor at 135 psi, which is what happens if the outlet is blocked (a deadhead), which is why fully closing BV-01 is dangerous for the tubing and the sensor.

How much flow you actually get depends on two curves. The pump curve says how much flow the pump can deliver against a given back pressure: 6.1 L/min against nothing (free flow), less as the back pressure rises, zero at the cutoff. The system curve says how much pressure your pipework needs to pass a given flow (idea 4). The loop settles where they cross, the operating point.

Closing a valve adds loss, so the system curve gets steeper and the operating point slides to lower flow. This picture explains three results in the guide: why flow falls when BV-01 closes (Q2.1 and condition B in Q3.2), why the ball valve's last 25 % of opening barely matters (by then the tube and sensor dominate the system curve), and why 6 L/min is hard to reach (the system curve always takes some pressure, so you never get the full free flow).

Speed control by PWM. The firmware sets each pump's speed with pulse-width modulation: it switches the 12 V on and off thousands of times a second. The fraction of time it is on is the duty cycle. At 50 % the motor sees, on average, about half the voltage and runs slower. Flow does not halve exactly, because the pump curve shifts down while the system curve stays the same.

Running dry. With no water inside, a pump has nothing to cool or cushion it and the diaphragm wears quickly. Air sucked in with the water makes the flow sputter, which is what condition E in Q3.2 looks like.

6. Valves and fittings

  • Ball valve (BV-01, BV-02, BV-03). A ball with a hole through it sits in the line; a quarter turn of the handle swings the hole from across the flow (shut) to in line with it (open). It is built for on/off duty and is a crude throttle, because most of the flow change happens in the first part of the turn. Engineers call this a quick-opening characteristic; the other common shapes are linear (flow proportional to opening) and equal-percentage (each extra bit of opening raises flow by the same fraction).
  • Needle valve. A tapered needle slides into a seat, giving fine, gradual control. The paper mentions one, but the kit has none, so BV-01 stands in for it.
  • Solenoid valve (SOV-01, also written XV-01 or OV-01). An electromagnet pulls a plunger off its seat when powered. Cheap 12 V valves like this one are almost always normally closed: shut with no power, open only while energised. That is fail-safe, because a power cut isolates the supply tank. You can confirm it by blowing gently through it unpowered. Solenoid valves of this kind usually need a little pressure difference across them to seal properly, so mount it with the arrow on its body pointing in the flow direction.
  • Tee (T-01). A three-way junction that merges two flows into one or splits one into two. In Case 2 it is where the flush line joins the main line.
  • Bulkhead fitting (B1 to B5). A threaded through-wall connector that lets a tube pass through a tank wall without leaking, sealed by a washer on each side.
  • Teflon (PTFE) tape. Wrapped clockwise around a male thread before assembly, it fills the gaps between threads so they do not weep.
  • Push-fit fitting. Push the tube in and a toothed collet grips it; press the collet ring to release. They hold well at the pressures in normal running but can let go at deadhead pressure.

7. Tanks, the sump, and the float switch

A sump is a low collection tank that other lines drain into. Its level obeys the mass balance from idea 2: the rate the volume changes equals flow in minus flow out.

Pour in 1 L suddenly (the paper's "external charge") and the level jumps; while P-01 is stopped, P-02 keeps removing about 3 L/min, so that extra litre is gone in about 20 s.

A float switch is a buoyant float on a hinge or stem carrying a magnet; when the water lifts it, the magnet closes a tiny sealed switch (a reed switch). It only says yes or no, "level above this point", so it is a digital signal. Near the switch point, ripples make it flick on and off rapidly, which is called chatter; the firmware fixes this by waiting until the float has stayed clear for 3 s before restarting P-01. Engineers call this kind of deliberate gap between "off" and "on again" hysteresis.

A tank being drained needs air to get in, or a vacuum forms and the flow stops. That is why the flush tank's unused top holes are left open as vents.

8. The flow sensor (FT-01)

Inside the YF-S401 is a small rotor with a magnet in it. Water spins the rotor, and a Hall-effect sensor (a chip that responds to a magnetic field) outputs one electrical pulse each time the magnet passes. More flow spins the rotor faster, so the number of pulses per second, the frequency f in hertz (Hz), rises in step with the flow. Over its working range the relationship is close to a straight line:

The datasheet value is K ≈ 98 Hz per L/min, which means about 5880 pulses per litre. Real sensors differ from the datasheet by several percent, and the number shifts with mounting, bubbles and temperature, which is why the paper insists on calibration: measuring pulses against a known volume yourself (Q2.3) and fitting your own a and b (Q2.2). The offset b exists because the rotor needs a little flow to overcome its own friction before it turns at all, which is also why the sensor's range starts at 0.3 L/min rather than zero.

Totalizing means adding up everything that has passed: count all pulses and divide by pulses per litre, or add up flow × time for each short interval. In industry a sensor that sends its reading on as a signal is called a transmitter, hence "flow transmitter, FT".

9. The electronics

  • SMPS (switch-mode power supply). Converts 230 V AC mains into steady 12 V DC. Electrical power is voltage × current (P = V × I), so three pumps at 3.5 A draw about 3 × 3.5 × 12 ≈ 126 W, which is why the supply must be big enough for Case 2.
  • Fuse. A deliberately weak link that melts and cuts the power if a short circuit makes the current spike.
  • ESP32 (microcontroller). A tiny computer on one chip that runs one program in a loop forever. Its pins, called GPIO (general-purpose input/output), can read on/off signals (the switch, the float) and output 3.3 V logic signals (pump speed, solenoid on/off). It can only supply a few milliamps from a pin, a thousand times too little for a 3 A pump, so it never powers anything directly; it only tells drivers what to do.
  • Interrupts. The flow sensor sends up to about 600 pulses a second. Rather than checking the pin constantly, the ESP32 uses an interrupt: a hardware trigger that pauses the main program for a microsecond to add one to a counter on every pulse, so none are missed.
  • Motor driver (BTS7960). A high-current switch board between the 12 V supply and a pump. Inside is an H-bridge: four power transistors arranged so the motor can be connected to 12 V either way round. Its logic pins come from the ESP32: R_EN and L_EN enable the two halves, and RPWM and LPWM carry the PWM signal for each direction. The pumps only run one way, so one PWM pin is used and the other held low. It is rated far above the pumps' 3.5 A, so it runs cool.
  • MOSFET module (D4184). A single electronic switch: when the ESP32 sets its input high, the transistor connects the solenoid coil to 12 V.
  • Flyback diode (1N4007). A coil resists sudden changes of current. When the MOSFET switches the solenoid off, the collapsing magnetic field produces a voltage spike that can destroy the transistor. A diode across the coil gives that current a harmless loop to die away in.
  • Pull-up and debouncing. A switch input is held at 3.3 V by a resistor (a pull-up); pressing the switch connects it to ground, so the program reads LOW. Mechanical contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when pressed, which would look like several presses, so the firmware ignores changes shorter than a few tens of milliseconds.
  • Serial monitor. The USB cable carries text between the ESP32 and a laptop. You type commands into it (trial start, fit, flow 3) and it streams the CSV log back.

10. Control logic

State machine. The firmware is always in exactly one named condition, such as idle, Case 1 running, P-01 held off for high sump, waiting for BV-02, flushing, or done. Events move it from one state to the next: the button press, the float tripping or clearing, a timer running out, or the flow staying at zero. Writing the sequence this way is what lets Case 1 and Case 2 run in one go with no human input beyond opening BV-02.

Open loop versus closed loop. Open loop means setting an output and accepting whatever happens: P-02 at 100 % gives whatever flow the operating point allows. Closed loop, or feedback control, means measuring the result and correcting the output: read the flow, compare it with the 3 L/min target, and nudge the pump speed. The firmware's flow command uses a PI controller. The P (proportional) part corrects in proportion to the current error. The I (integral) part adds up past errors, so a small leftover error keeps growing its correction until it is gone.

Interlocks. Automatic protective stops built into the logic: P-01 stops on high sump level, everything stops when flow stays near zero in the flush, and a 600 s cap stops the flush even if the zero-flow check fails.

11. Measurement and the statistics in Q2.2

  • Mean and spread. Readings wobble, so report the average over a period (the mean) and how far readings strayed from it (the minimum and maximum, or the standard deviation).
  • Random versus systematic error. Random error scatters readings both ways and shrinks when you average or repeat; examples are reaction time when swinging the tube, or reading a jug's markings. Systematic error pushes every reading the same way and does not average out; an example is using the datasheet's 98 when your sensor is really 92. Calibration removes systematic error; repeats reduce random error.
  • Linear regression (least squares). Given scattered points, the best straight line is the one that makes the sum of the squared vertical gaps between points and line as small as possible. Its slope is a and its intercept (where it crosses the Q axis) is b. The formulas in Q2.2 compute exactly that, and so do Excel's SLOPE and INTERCEPT and the firmware's fit command.
  • R² (coefficient of determination). The fraction of the variation in Q that the straight line explains. 1 is a perfect line; above 0.99 is excellent for this kind of sensor; much lower means a bad trial or a sensor that is not linear over the range used.
  • Percent error. How far the line's prediction is from the measured value, as a share of the measured value: |predicted − measured| / measured × 100 %. The worst trial gives the maximum error and the average of all trials gives the average error.

12. Residence time and fault diagnosis

Residence time is how long, on average, a bit of liquid spends inside a volume: the volume divided by the flow through it (Q3.1 has the full answer). It is also the time to replace a volume's contents once, which is why a flush must run for several residence times to clear the old fluid out.

Diagnosis is working backwards from a symptom to a cause. The difficulty is that different causes can produce the same symptom: zero pulses from FT-01 can mean a dead pump, a blocked line or a dead sensor. To tell them apart you need a second, independent measurement that the causes affect differently, such as pump current, pressure, or a tank level. Engineers call a system observable when its sensors are enough to tell its possible states apart; Q3.2 is really asking where your kit is not observable and what you would add to fix that.

13. Reading a P&ID

A P&ID (piping and instrumentation diagram) is the map of a process: every tank, pump, valve and instrument, the pipes between them, and the signal links to the controller. It shows connections, not physical layout or scale. Each item gets a tag: letters say what it is, the number says which one. The letter codes follow the ISA-5.1 standard.

Tag Read as In this kit
TK Tank TK-01 process tank, TK-02 sump, TK-03 flush tank
P Pump P-01 transfer, P-02 return, P-03 flush
BV Ball valve BV-01 throttle, BV-02 flush isolation, BV-03 maintenance
SOV / XV Solenoid or on-off valve SOV-01
FT Flow (F) transmitter (T) FT-01, the YF-S401
LS Level (L) switch (S) LS-01, the float switch
T Tee T-01

On the drawing, solid lines are pipes, arrows show flow direction, dashed lines are electrical signals, and instruments are drawn as small circles (bubbles) with their tag inside.

Glossary

Term Meaning
Bulkhead Leak-tight connector through a tank wall
Calibration Measuring a sensor against a known reference and fitting the conversion from its output to the true value
Cavitation Vapour bubbles forming where pressure drops too low at a pump inlet, then collapsing; causes noise and erratic flow
Check valve One-way valve; diaphragm pumps contain two
Deadhead Running a pump against a closed outlet, so pressure climbs to the pump's maximum
Duty cycle Percentage of time a PWM signal is on
Flush Pushing clean liquid through the lines to clear out the previous fluid or debris
Free flow A pump's flow with nothing resisting it, 6.1 L/min here
GPIO A microcontroller pin that can read or set an on/off signal
Hall effect A voltage that appears in a chip when a magnetic field passes, used to detect the rotor's magnet
Hysteresis A deliberate gap between the switch-off and switch-on points so a signal does not flicker
Interlock An automatic protective stop built into the control logic
Priming Filling a pump and its inlet line with liquid so it can pump
PWM Pulse-width modulation, fast on-off switching to set an average power
Skid A frame-mounted package of process equipment
Sump A low collection tank other lines drain into
Throttling Partly closing a valve to reduce flow
Totalizer A running count of the total volume that has passed a flow sensor
